title: When ranking a candidate higher makes them lose
description:
Seventeen coworkers ranked three lunch spots. Tacos won.

Gita and Hugo ranked Tacos dead last — they can't stand tacos. Watch them get a better lunch by voting as though Tacos were their favorite.

In the what-ifs explorer, move Tacos to the top of Gita's and Hugo's ballots. Nothing else changes, and the only change helps Tacos — so Tacos loses. Two first preferences lighter, Pizza now trails Sushi and is eliminated first; Pizza's voters flow to Sushi, and Sushi wins 9–8. Gita and Hugo traded their worst outcome for their second favorite by lying about their first.

That is non-monotonicity: under instant-runoff, gaining support can cost a candidate the election, because first preferences decide who gets eliminated. And wherever that is true, an honest ballot is not always your best one.

lesson.summary: Two Pizza voters move Tacos from last to first. That is the only change, and it only helps Tacos — so Tacos loses to Sushi.
